summary: Describes how an EPP session is mapped onto a single TCP connection. It requires Transport Layer Security to protect the information exchanged between EPP client and server. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: EPP needs a road to travel on. This document says it travels on a single TCP connection that is wrapped in a protective tunnel so nobody can peek.

questions: how does epp run over tcp
how are epp messages framed over tcp
subtitle: How EPP runs over one TCP connection, with a 4-byte length prefix and mandatory TLS.

tldr.problem: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) needs a transport that carries its XML commands and responses and keeps its sessions intact, and EPP alone sends client passwords in plain text.
tldr.mechanism: Each EPP session maps to a single TCP connection. Every message is framed with a 32-bit total length, and the connection MUST be protected with TLS using mutual certificate authentication.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 4934 and is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5734 is an Internet Standard (STD 69) published in August 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4934 and is updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Sessions and Connections
sections.content:
An EPP session maps onto a single client-server TCP connection. The client is the peer that opens the connection and the server is the peer that answers. The server MUST listen on a standard TCP port assigned by IANA, and the client makes an active OPEN call to that port. Once the TCP session is up, the server MUST send an EPP <greeting>.

A session normally ends when the client sends an EPP <logout> command. The server then MUST end the session and close the connection. A client MAY also end a session by closing the connection. A server MAY limit how long a connection lives. It MAY close one that has been idle for a server-defined period, or one that has been open for longer than a server-defined period.
sections.plainLanguage: You call the server, and it says hello first. When you say goodbye, it hangs up. It may also hang up on you if you stay quiet for too long.

sections.title: Message Exchange
sections.content:
Except for the server greeting, EPP messages start with a client command, and the server MUST return the response on the same TCP connection that carried the command. A client MUST NOT spread the commands of one session over several connections. It MAY open several connections for several sessions, one per session, and a server SHOULD limit how many it allows.

EPP is a command-response protocol: one command, one response. A client MAY gain a little speed by pipelining, which means sending more than one command before the first response arrives. This does not change the one-command, one-response mode of the core protocol. Each data unit MUST contain a single EPP message, so combining several commands in one data unit is not allowed. Commands MUST be processed independently and in the order sent.

If the connection drops after a server has processed a command but before the response is delivered, the server MAY try to undo the effects. EPP commands are idempotent, so running one more than once has the same net effect as running it once. A server SHOULD also set a time limit for a client to issue a well-formed command, and SHOULD end the session and close the connection if it is exceeded.
sections.plainLanguage: You may ask several questions in a row without waiting for each answer, but each question goes in its own envelope. The answers come back in the same order, on the same line.

sections.title: The Data Unit Format
sections.content:
Each EPP data unit has two fields: a 32-bit header giving the Total Length of the data unit, followed by the EPP XML instance. The length is in octets, in network (big endian) byte order, and it includes the four octets of the length field itself. A receiver finds the size of the XML by subtracting four from the total length, and it must read that many octets before it processes the message.

This explicit count is how the RFC frames messages on a TCP byte stream, which has no message boundaries of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with a number that says how long it is, counting the number itself. The listener reads that many bytes and knows exactly where one message ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EPP by itself offers only simple client authentication with identifiers and plain text passwords. A passive attack is enough to learn them, which allows trivial command forgery. So protection against most other attacks MUST come from layered protocols.

Over TCP, TLS 1.0 or a successor such as TLS 1.2, using the latest version both sides support, MUST provide integrity, confidentiality and mutual strong client-server authentication. A weak cryptographic mode that some TLS implementations contain SHOULD NOT be used. The TLS certificate identifies the machines, and the EPP client identifier and password still identify the user. The two identities can differ. Acceptable certificate identities MUST be agreed out of band, and the presented identities MUST match before EPP service is granted.

Before sending credentials, a client needs to check that the server certificate and the EPP greeting are what it expects. It MUST compare the certificate subject or subjectAltName to its expected server identity and abort on a mismatch. The RFC also warns that EPP TCP servers are open to common denial-of-service attacks such as TCP SYN flooding. It suggests firewalls and border router filters that restrict inbound access to known, trusted clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain EPP is like shouting your password across a room. So the call is wrapped in a scrambler, and both sides show ID cards before any talking starts.

sections.title: The TLS Usage Profile
sections.content:
The client connects, sends the TLS Client Hello to begin the handshake, and may send its first EPP message when the handshake finishes. TLS implementations are REQUIRED to support the mandatory cipher suite of the version they implement: TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA for TLS 1.0, TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA for TLS 1.1 and TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA for TLS 1.2. The profile is assumed to apply to future TLS versions too.

Mutual authentication is REQUIRED. Signatures on the whole certification path for both machines, and details such as validity periods and machine names, MUST be validated. EPP service MUST NOT be granted until the handshake and certificate validation have succeeded.

The client checks the server name or IP address against the server certificate. For a name, it uses a dNSName subjectAltName if present, with an asterisk wildcard allowed only as the left-most label. So *.example.com matches a.example.com but not example.com or a.b.example.com. The Common Name is a deprecated fallback. For an IP address the client uses the iPAddress subjectAltName, which is four octets for IPv4 and sixteen for IPv6. All EPP messages MUST be sent as TLS application data, and a server that closes an idle connection MUST try to exchange close_notify alerts first.
sections.plainLanguage: Before talking, both sides show ID cards and the client checks that the server's card matches the name it dialled. After that, every EPP message travels inside the scrambled call.
